frozen_original.title: Linda McMahon Cuts Education Department Staff by 45%, Transfers Programs Without Authorization
frozen_original.synopsis: Education Secretary Linda McMahon oversaw a reduction of Department of Education staff from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to 2,300 — a 45% cut. More than 100 programs and department obligations were offloaded to other federal agencies, including elementary and secondary education programs moved to the Department of Labor and family engagement efforts transferred to HHS. McMahon testified before a House Education hearing: "It is the mission to shut down the bureaucracy of the Department of Education." The proposed FY2027 budget called for a $12 billion (15%) reduction in education funding. McMahon's strategy involved making all interagency transfer agreements temporary to shield them from legal challenge. Democrats accused McMahon of "dismantling one of the country's strongest civil rights institutions."
frozen_original.rationale: Systematic dismantlement of the Education Department — transferring programs without congressional authorization, slashing staff, cutting funding — undermines educational equity for millions of children. The deliberate strategy of making transfers "temporary" to evade legal accountability reveals awareness these actions may be unlawful.

primary.split_explanation: The frozen record combines separate workforce changes, the November 2025 interagency agreements, and a later June 2026 agreement announcement. These three children isolate separately dated, source-supported actions. The unsupported FY2027 $12 billion/15% figure is omitted; the May 2026 hearing is context in the staffing report, not a separate child event. The claimed total of more than 100 transferred programs is not carried forward because the retrieved official releases describe separate agreements and retain ED oversight or statutory authority.

counterpart_review.result: A scan of all supplied worker input rows found no other Education Department staffing or interagency-agreement card for these dates. The reviewed entries concern a William E. Henry pardon, an unrelated Epstein-files allegation, other clemency matters, and 2018 recipient claims; none is a duplicate of these education actions.

children.description_short: An NPR report citing OPM data said the Education Department's headcount fell from about 4,200 in 2024 to 2,300 in 2026.
children.description_medium: An NPR story carried by KPBS reported that the U.S. Department of Education had roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 and 2,300 in 2026, a decline of about 45%, citing Office of Personnel Management data. The figures were reported during a May 2026 congressional hearing. The source does not give exact dates for either headcount or measure service effects.
children.description_long: An NPR story republished by KPBS on May 14, 2026 reported that the U.S. Department of Education's workforce had fallen from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to 2,300 in 2026, citing Office of Personnel Management data. The story described the difference as a roughly 45% reduction. It placed the figures in a House education committee hearing where Education Secretary Linda McMahon defended the administration's approach to shrinking the department and shifting some work. This card separates the staff comparison from distinct interagency agreements and budget proposals that had been bundled in the original record. The article does not give exact dates for the two OPM counts, identify which reductions came through layoffs rather than attrition, or quantify resulting service delays or student outcomes. It supports the approximate headcount comparison and the report date; it does not establish why each position ended or measure the effect on students. May 14 is the article's publication date, not a claim that all reductions happened that day.

children.title: Education Department Announces Six Interagency Agreements on November 18, 2025
children.description_short: Education announced six interagency agreements with Labor, Interior, HHS, and State to change administration of selected federal education programs.
children.description_medium: On November 18, 2025, the Education Department announced six interagency agreements with Labor, Interior, HHS, and State. The release described partner-agency roles in selected programs. For the K-12 agreement, it said Labor would manage competitions and provide technical assistance under Education Department oversight. It did not establish a transfer of statutory authority.
children.description_long: On November 18, 2025, the U.S. Department of Education announced six interagency agreements with the Departments of Labor, Interior, Health and Human Services, and State. The announcement described the agreements as changing administration of selected federal education programs and assigned partner agencies greater management roles. For the K-12 partnership, it said Labor would manage competitions and provide technical assistance with Education Department oversight. This card isolates that dated announcement from the June 2026 agreements and the separate staffing decline. The release does not substantiate the original record's claim that more than 100 programs were transferred without authorization. It describes interagency program management, and its K-12 section expressly says the arrangement remains under Education Department oversight. The release does not establish repeal of the department, transfer of its statutory policymaking authority, or the proposed FY2027 budget figure. The date is the official announcement date; this record concerns the agreements, not a later outcome measure.

children.title: Education Announces Four New Agreements on Disability Programs and Civil Rights
children.description_short: On June 16, 2026, Education announced four agreements with HHS and DOJ covering disability programs, civil-rights enforcement, and related services.
children.description_medium: On June 16, 2026, the Education Department announced four interagency agreements with HHS and DOJ. The release says HHS will partner on special education and rehabilitative services and DOJ on civil-rights enforcement, student privacy, and training. It says federal civil-rights enforcement will continue without interruption and ED will retain its statutory authority.
children.description_long: On June 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education announced four new interagency agreements with the Departments of Health and Human Services and Justice. The release says HHS will partner with Education on special education and rehabilitative services, while DOJ will partner on civil-rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services. The announcement states that federal civil-rights enforcement will continue without interruption and that the Education Department will retain all statutory authorities and functions. This card records the agreement announcement and its stated scope. It does not describe a completed transfer of statutory authority, a loss of all federal business or education support, or measurable effects on students and families. The source says these agreements followed 10 partnerships signed over the prior year; that broader history is not counted here. This entry focuses on the June 16 action rather than combining it with the November 2025 agreements, the staffing comparison, or a proposed FY2027 budget reduction. Later implementation evidence would be needed to quantify operational changes or outcomes.

frozen_original.title: Trump DOJ Opens Investigations Into George Soros, ActBlue, and Political Enemies
frozen_original.synopsis: The Trump Justice Department under Attorney General Pam Bondi opened formal investigations in early March 2025 into progressive organizations including George Soros's Open Society Foundations and the Democratic Party's main small-dollar fundraising platform, ActBlue. The investigations were widely seen as weaponized use of the DOJ to target political opponents and donors. Former prosecutors from both parties condemned the investigations as resembling banana republic tactics of using criminal law to punish political enemies. Civil rights groups noted the investigations mirrored tactics used by authoritarian governments to suppress political opposition. No credible predicate for criminal investigation of the organizations had been publicly identified.

primary.split_reason: The frozen entry combines two separately dated matters: an April 24 presidential memorandum about online fundraising allegations and a September 25 reported DOJ planning directive concerning Open Society Foundations. The first source is an official memorandum; the later matter is attributed to Reuters and The Hill reporting. No source supports a simultaneous early-March opening of formal investigations.

children.title: Trump Directed DOJ to Investigate Allegations About Online Fundraising Platforms
children.description_short: Trump's April 24 memo directed DOJ and Treasury to investigate allegations about online fundraising platforms and cited ActBlue-related findings; it did not establish wrongdoing.
children.description_medium: On April 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum directing the attorney general, in consultation with Treasury, to investigate allegations involving straw or foreign contributions through online fundraising platforms. The memorandum cited congressional findings involving ActBlue, and Reuters reported that the directive targeted ActBlue and other platforms. The sources document the order and its allegations, not criminal findings or proof of misconduct.
children.description_long: On April 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum directing the attorney general, in consultation with the Treasury secretary, to use lawful authority to investigate allegations that online fundraising platforms were used to make straw or foreign political contributions. The White House memorandum cited congressional findings about ActBlue and described suspected activity; it also directed the attorney general to report results within 180 days. Reuters reported that the memorandum targeted Democratic fundraising group ActBlue and other online platforms. The available sources establish the presidential directive and the allegations it cited. They do not establish that ActBlue committed a crime or that an investigation produced findings. This action occurred on April 24, not in early March. The original entry's assertion that DOJ simultaneously opened formal investigations of ActBlue and Open Society Foundations is not supported by this memorandum. Reporting about Open Society Foundations appeared months later and is represented in a separate child record. This description does not present the memo's allegations as proven facts.

children.title: DOJ Official Reportedly Asked Prosecutors to Prepare Plans to Investigate Open Society Foundations
children.description_short: On Sept. 25, reports said DOJ asked U.S. attorneys to prepare investigative plans concerning OSF; no findings or charges were reported.
children.description_medium: On September 25, 2025, Reuters and The Hill reported that a Justice Department official had asked several U.S. attorneys' offices to prepare plans to investigate Open Society Foundations. The reports described a planning directive and possible charges under consideration, not a confirmed formal case, filed charges, or findings. OSF called the reported push politically motivated and said its work was lawful.
children.description_long: On September 25, 2025, Reuters reported that a senior Justice Department official had instructed several U.S. attorneys' offices to draft plans for an investigation of Open Society Foundations (OSF). The report, based on an earlier New York Times account, said the directive suggested possible charges, including arson and material support for terrorism. The Hill reported that an attorney in Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office sent a note asking prosecutors to prepare for investigations. These reports describe a request to prepare plans; they do not establish that prosecutors opened a formal case, filed charges, or found wrongdoing. Reuters said OSF described the reported push as politically motivated and stated that its activities were peaceful and lawful; that is OSF's response, not an adjudicated finding about motive. The date is late September 2025, months after Trump's April memorandum about online fundraising platforms. The supplied combined record placed the ActBlue and OSF matters together under an early-March date; available reporting supports treating this later reported directive as a separate event and correcting that timeline. No investigation outcome is established in the sources cited here.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires FISA Court Judges Who Ruled Against Surveillance Requests
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration moved to remove judges from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court — a specialized federal court that reviews government applications to conduct domestic intelligence surveillance — after those judges issued rulings rejecting or conditioning certain surveillance requests the administration considered politically important. The FISA Court is composed of sitting federal district court judges designated by the Chief Justice of the United States; removing FISA Court judges without cause had no precedent in the court's history since its creation in 1978. The firings were described by intelligence community veterans and civil liberties advocates as an attempt to pack a specialized court with judges guaranteed to approve surveillance of the administration's political opponents. The Senate Judiciary Committee opened investigations into the removals, and the Chief Justice was formally asked to respond to the situation.
